newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-Hellaby still in acquiring mode.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Hellaby still in acquiring mode.

text.p: Hellaby Holdings Ltd is still in an acquiring mode despite being in the midst of a NZ$21.9 million share buyback, but no fresh initiatives are imminent, Managing Director Tur Borren said on Tuesday.
"New investments are always difficult to plan for and it's difficult to predict when they will happen," Borren told Reuters in an interview.
Hellaby sought situations where there was conflict between existing ownership and managements, and had a preference for manufacturing or distribution.
While the Hellaby's businesses had enjoyed the fruits of a strong economy, economic strength did not necessarily provide ideal buying opportunities.
Hellaby rules out investment in property, merchant banking and services and has a strong focus on New Zealand.

Borren said Hellaby's philosophy was in a way shaped by the mistakes of other local corporates, who had over-invested in their businesses to the point where they became larger than the small New Zealand market could cope with.
Similarly, Hellaby was a reluctant overseas investor, where New Zealand's performance had been "dreadful".

"We try and avoid those two things - over-resourcing our companies for the size of the New Zealand markets and investing overseas. We become involved in the ownership of real businesses where we think we can make a contribution," he said.

Hellaby's largest company is AB Equipment, an importer of forklift trucks and construction equipment with turnover of more than NZ$50 million. Brake and Transmission, a brake and clutch distributor, has turnover of $34 million.
Hellaby also has a 51 percent interest in Wellington retailer Kirkcaldie and Stains, with turnover of NZ$30.1 million.
It has several other medium and small sized investments.

"We say if we've got a company to a point where we think it is a leader in the New Zealand market, we take the money out and either give it back to our shareholders or indeed re-invest it in a business where we think, in a different sector of the market, we can repeat the exercise all over again.
"There is never a time when there are not companies out there that we are maybe having some disucssions with and you never know whether one is going to roll or not," he said.
Hellaby, which made a net profit fo NZ$14.6 million in the year to June, has been on a strong growth path for two years, earning between 24-25 cents a share.
Borren said 30 cents would be the next challenge.
The company, formerly Renouf Corp Ltd, has around NZ$63 million of tax losses available to it, plus some $14-15 million in deferred tax.

This means the company is not paying imputation tax credits, but Borren said it was contemplating ways of paying tax on behalf of shareholders, which would preserve its tax losses even longer and provide an advantage to shareholders.
